newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE-Venezuela election race stuff of soaps.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Venezuela election race stuff of soaps.

text.p: A former beauty queen leads in the polls. A failed coup leader has vowed to take power through the ballot box. And a disgraced former president has served notice that his political career is not finished.

With 18 months to presidential elections, the political scene has all the makings of one of Venezuela's celebrated soap operas. But the plethora of candidates and paucity of ideas could signal a sea-change in the country's political map as voters turn away from the two traditional parties that have dominated for five decades, analysts and politicians said.

"There's more talk about polls than about ideas," said Senator Eduardo Gomez Tamayo, a member of the ruling Convergence Party. "It's obvious that there has been a change in attitude. People are more demanding about what they expect," the former president of Congress added.

The new popular mood has parties scurrying for candidates who can catch a jaded public's imagination. Social democratic Democratic Action (AD) and social Christian Copei are the dominant forces in Venezuelan politics but the level of disillusionment has forced even these parties to widen their nets for potential candidates.
"There's a frantic-ness, a sense of casting about," independent political consultant Erik Ekvall said.

Nowhere is the search more intense than in Copei, which has not won a presidential election since Luis Herrera Campins' triumph in 1978. At a recent soul-searching weekend, Copei top brass agreed an outsider could become its candidate.
"Copei's opening up is interesting, though it is an admission of its own weakness," said Claudio Fermin, AD presidential candidate in 1993 and a front-runner to lead that party in 1998.
EX-MISS UNIVERSE TOPS PARTY LIST

Top of Copei's shopping list appears to be former Miss Universe Irene Saez, who dominates the pre-election debate. Saez, who is only 35, has become the candidate to beat. Overwhelmingly re-elected mayor of Caracas district Chacao in 1995, she tops opinion polls with 40 to 50 percent of popular support. Her closest rival gets only around 10 percent.

Saez makes little secret of her desire for the country's top job but has been careful not to make her bid official and to maintain her edge as an independent. "People are waiting for a political leader, a messiah ... and I'm realising that people are pointing to me," she told Reuters recently.

Critics say the statuesque blonde has no concrete policies and limited experience. But analysts said a Saez candidacy, backed by Copei or by a range of other parties, is almost a certainty, if only as an outlet for popular discontent.

"If Irene didn't exist we would have to invent her," political analyst Anibal Romero said in a newspaper interview. "She personifies aspirations which don't have alternative channels. That's why she heads the polls."

Saez' name is not the only one to come out of the political outfield as a potential candidate. Luis Giusti, who has led an unprecedented opening of the state oil industry as president of Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) has been mentioned by Copei and union-based Radical Cause (Causa R) politicians.
STRANGE POLITICAL BEDFELLOWS
In a country where ideological boundaries between parties are blurred, "you could see some very strange bedfellows," Ekvall said.

Retired Lt. Col. Hugo Chavez, leader of a failed 1992 coup attempt, and Perez, who completed a 28-month sentence under house arrest last September, also plan to join the electoral fray, although most analysts see their impact as small.

But, despite the novelty of non-traditional politicians, voters are turning off in increasing numbers, convinced that none of the potential candidates has what it takes to lead the once-rich nation back to prosperity.
"They're all interested in one thing -- themselves. Even Irene," housewife Maira Rivas said.

Voter apathy would play into the hands of AD as the only party with a machine capable of really delivering votes. AD candidates, backed by the most sophisticated party apparatus in the country, swept more than half the state governorships in 1995 local elections when turnout was less than 40 percent.

The Saez phenomenon is seen by many as a reaction to President Rafael Caldera. Although he broke with Copei to lead Convergence to power in 1993, the 81-year-old leader is seen as the creator of the much-maligned political establishment.
MOULD WAS SHATTERED IN 1988

South America's longest running democracy, Venezuela enjoyed relative political stability through a pact between Copei and AD to alternate power every five years. But the mould was broken with Carlos Andres Perez' second victory in 1988.

Tough economic reforms provoked bloody riots just weeks after Perez assumed power and two coup attempts in 1992. Confidence in the political system was rocked further when he was forced out of office in 1993, just eight months before completing his term, to face corruption charges.

Caldera, who has run for president in every election he has been eligible for since dictator Gen. Marcos Perez Jimeez was toppled in 1958, was elected on a ticket of honesty and social welfare. But his inability to cope with a massive financial sector crisis and perceived corruption in the public sector has seen his popularity plummet from more than 70 percent to less than 30 percent.
The failure of the grandfather of Venezuelan politics to restore confidence in the system could be the beginning of the end for the old parties.
"We're in the middle of something, between the death of one system and the birth of another," Ekvall said.
With the Causa R and Movement to Socialism (MAS) parties split internally, AD continues to hold most of the cards, particularly if voter disinterest continues, analysts said.
